content: Lung transplantation is a widely accepted and effective treatment for patients with end-stage lung diseases. However, recipients of lung transplants face a significant risk of organ rejection, necessitating lifelong immunosuppressive therapy. It is critical to establish a safe and effective immunosuppressive treatment strategy for these patients. Currently, there is no consensus on the use of T-cell-targeting immunosuppressive antibodies for induction therapy following lung transplantation. The objective of this review was to evaluate the potential benefits and harms of T-cell antibody induction therapy using agents such as antithymocyte globulin (ATG), antilymphocyte globulin (ALG), interleukin-2 receptor antagonists (IL-2RA), alemtuzumab, or muromonab-CD3 in lung transplant recipients. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted in the Cochrane Renal Group's Specialised Register up to March 4, 2013. This database includes studies identified through systematic searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared monoclonal or polyclonal T-cell antibody induction therapies in lung transplant recipients. A key inclusion criterion was that all participants within each study received the same maintenance immunosuppressive therapy. Three authors independently extracted data from the included studies. Risk ratios (RR) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and mean differences (MD) were calculated for continuous outcomes, both with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the Cochrane risk of bias tool, and trial sequential analyses were performed to evaluate the risk of random errors. The review included six RCTs involving a total of 278 adult lung transplant recipients. These studies assessed the use of T-cell antibody induction therapy. All included studies were found to have a high risk of bias. The comparisons made in the review included the following: 1. Polyclonal or monoclonal T-cell antibody induction versus no induction (3 studies, 140 participants). 2. Polyclonal T-cell antibody induction versus no induction (3 studies, 125 participants). 3. IL-2RA versus no induction (1 study, 25 participants). 4. Polyclonal T-cell antibody induction versus muromonab-CD3 (1 study, 64 participants). 5. Polyclonal T-cell antibody induction versus IL-2RA (3 studies, 100 participants). Overall, no significant differences were observed between the interventions in terms of mortality, acute rejection, adverse effects, infections, pneumonia, cytomegalovirus infection, bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease, or cancer. However, one study comparing antithymocyte globulin (ATG) to muromonab-CD3 reported a higher incidence of adverse events in the ATG group (74% vs. 40%; RR 1.84, 95% CI 1.13 to 2.98). Despite this finding, trial sequential analysis indicated that the required information size had not been reached, and the cumulative Z-curve did not cross the trial sequential alpha-spending monitoring boundaries, limiting the reliability of this result. None of the included studies reported outcomes related to quality of life or kidney injury. Furthermore, trial sequential analyses revealed that none of the meta-analyses reached the required information sizes, and the cumulative Z-curves did not cross the trial sequential alpha-spending monitoring boundaries or enter the area of futility. In conclusion, this review did not identify clear benefits or harms associated with T-cell antibody induction therapy compared to no induction or when different types of T-cell antibodies were compared. The number of studies, participants, and reported outcomes was limited, and all included studies were at high risk of methodological bias. Further well-designed RCTs are needed to robustly evaluate the benefits and harms of T-cell antibody induction therapy in lung transplant recipients. Future studies should adhere to rigorous methodologies to minimize the risks of systematic and random errors.
